title: Media & Info Check
goal: Your kid learns to check before they believe or share. Faced with a post, a photo or a video, they pause when it makes them feel a lot, find out who made it, look closely for signs it was edited or made by AI, search for it somewhere else, and decide: real, fake or not sure yet.
need: A screen you can look at together
A few videos, photos or posts to check, real and fake
A search engine, with you beside them

academics.text: spotting edits in photos and videos

levelsLine: Every step has three levels: Explore, Develop, Extend. Pick the one that fits your kid today, and change it anytime. Siblings can do the same step at different levels, side by side.

howTo.intro: The trap is a list of warnings about the internet. Your job is to check things together, out loud, so they hear how you think, and to make 'let's check' sound fun, not scary.

plan.what: Practise on a few examples you pick (Steps 1 to 3).
Use the same checks on anything that surprises them.

troubleshoot.q: They think everything is fake now
troubleshoot.a: Check a real one too. The goal is checking, not doubting everything: most things they see are real.
Say so. 'I'm not sure, let's look it up' is the most useful thing they can hear from you.
Stop and talk about it. Checking whether something is real can wait until they feel okay.

lesson.text: Fakes are made to make you feel something fast: wow, scared, angry. That feeling is the signal to slow down. A few quick checks, like who made it, what looks off and where else it shows up, usually tell you if it's real.
lesson.before: 'It's a video, so it must be real.'

model.line: A shark swimming down a flooded highway. Wow.
A stranger's post, no news site.
The same shark, after hurricanes years apart.

lesson.modelNote: This picture goes around after almost every big hurricane. One search shows the same shark in floods years apart, which is the clue that it was made up.

steps.title: Pause when you feel it
steps.why: Fakes work by making you feel something before you think. The feeling is the signal.
steps.kid: Your kid looks at an example you picked and notices how it makes them feel, using the Pause signals card in the Check It Toolkit at the end of the guide: wow, scared, angry or 'I have to show someone'.
steps.you: Say what you feel too: 'Whoa, that's amazing. That makes me want to check it.' Make the pause sound normal, not suspicious.
ask: How does this make you feel?
Do you want to show someone right now?
steps.tip: The stronger the feeling, the more important the check. 'Too amazing' is a clue.

levels.explore: Show with a face how the video makes you feel, then say 'Let's check.'
levels.develop: Name the feeling, and say what the post wants you to do.
levels.extend: Find the exact words or moment designed to make you feel that way.

steps.title: Find out who made it
steps.why: Who posted it, and why, says a lot about whether to trust it.
steps.kid: Your kid finds who posted or made it, using the Who made it card: a news site, a company, a stranger, an AI tool, or nobody they can find.
steps.you: Show them where to look: the name, the account, the website, the date. Read it out loud together.
ask: What do they want you to do or believe?
steps.tip: No name, no date and no source is a clue in itself.

levels.explore: Find the name of who posted it, with a parent.
levels.develop: Find who made it, when, and why they might have made it.
levels.extend: Compare two accounts that posted the same thing, and which one to trust more.

steps.title: Look closely
steps.why: Edited and AI-made photos and videos often slip on small details.
steps.kid: Your kid looks for clues using the Look closely card: hands and faces, edges and shadows, writing in the background, voices that don't match lips.
steps.you: Pause the video and zoom in together. Point out one clue, then let them find the next.
ask: What looks strange if you zoom in?
Does anything move or sound wrong?
steps.tip: Good fakes can pass this test. If nothing looks off, it still needs Step 4.

levels.explore: Spot one thing that looks strange, like a hand or a shadow.
levels.develop: Check every clue on the Look closely card, and mark what you find.
levels.extend: Compare a real photo and an AI-made one side by side, and list the differences.

steps.title: Search for it somewhere else
steps.why: Real news shows up in more than one place. Fakes usually don't, or they show up as 'fake'.
steps.kid: Your kid searches for it, using the Check elsewhere card: a few key words with 'fake' or 'fact check', a trusted news site, or an image search.
steps.you: Do the first search together, and show them how to spot a fact-checking site.
ask: Where else does this show up?
steps.tip: If the same photo shows up years earlier, or in a different story, it's been reused.

levels.explore: Watch a parent search, and say what you see.
levels.develop: Search for it in two different ways, and note what you find.
levels.extend: Find where it first came from, and how it changed as people shared it.

steps.title: Decide, then share or wait
steps.why: Checking only matters if it changes what you do next.
steps.kid: Your kid decides, using the Decide card: real, fake or not sure yet. Then they choose what to do: share it, don't share it, or wait and check later.
steps.you: Respect 'not sure yet'. It's the right answer more often than people think.
ask: Real, fake or not sure yet?
What would happen if you shared it and it was fake?
steps.tip: 'Not sure yet' means don't share yet. That one habit stops most fakes.

levels.explore: Say real, fake or not sure, and why.
levels.develop: Decide, then explain your three best clues to someone at home.
levels.extend: Check three things you see this week, and tell the family which ones fooled you at first.

reference.title: Check It Toolkit
reference.intro: When to pause, what to look for, where to check, and how to decide.

items.name: Pause signals

lines.v: too amazing to be true
it makes you worried or afraid
it makes you mad at someone
'Share before it's deleted!'

items.ask: Which feeling fools you most easily?

items.name: Who made it

lines.v: a person, a news site, a company?
is it new, or old and reshared?
to inform, to sell, to get clicks?
does it say it was made with AI?

items.ask: Which source would you trust most?

items.name: Look closely

lines.v: extra fingers, blurry teeth, odd eyes
smudged outlines, shadows going the wrong way
signs and letters that don't make sense
voices that don't match the lips

items.ask: Which clue is hardest to spot?

items.name: Check elsewhere

lines.v: key words plus 'fake' or 'fact check'
a trusted news site you know
has this picture been used before?
two places that don't copy each other

items.ask: Which check would you try first?

items.name: Decide

lines.v: a trusted source, and it shows up elsewhere
clues, reused, or called fake by fact-checkers
don't share yet
only what you'd stand behind

conclusion.headline: They check before they believe, or share.
conclusion.text: Notice the next time they see something amazing on a screen. If their first words are 'is that real?' or 'let's check', the pause is becoming a habit.
conclusion.celebrate: When they catch a fake, or choose not to share something they're unsure about, say: 'That pause just stopped a fake from spreading.'
extensions: Make a family 'fooled me' list of fakes you've each believed
Make an obviously fake photo together with a simple editing tool, and see who can spot the clues
Look at the same news story on two different sites, and compare how they tell it
Ask a grandparent how they checked news before the internet

signs: They ask 'is that real?' on their own
They look for who made something before believing it
They wait instead of sharing when they're unsure
makeItReal: The next time a video or post surprises your family, stop and check it together, out loud, before anyone shares it.
